questions.q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol), in the terms this lesson uses?
options: An open standard for how an AI agent discovers and calls tools exposed by a server
A type of SQL join used only in Cortex queries
A billing plan tier for Cortex functions
questions.explain: MCP acts as a common 'plug shape' so any MCP-aware client can call any MCP-aware server's tools without custom per-pair integration code.

questions.q: Which of the following tools does the Snowflake-managed MCP server expose?
options: CORTEX_ANALYST_MESSAGE, for natural-language-to-SQL over a semantic view
A tool for editing video files
A tool for managing email inboxes
A tool exclusively for resetting user passwords
questions.explain: The managed server bundles CORTEX_AGENT_RUN, CORTEX_ANALYST_MESSAGE, CORTEX_SEARCH_SERVICE_QUERY, SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL, and custom GENERIC tools.

questions.q: Which MCP capabilities does this lesson say the Snowflake-managed server does NOT support?
questions.explain: The server is scoped specifically to tool discovery and invocation; resources, prompts, roots, and notifications from the broader MCP spec are not implemented.

questions.q: Under which permissions does a tool call made through the MCP server execute?
options: The caller's own Snowflake role, so existing RBAC, masking, and row-access policies apply automatically
A universal admin role with no restrictions
No permissions are checked once OAuth succeeds
A role chosen at random for each request
questions.explain: Because tool calls run under the caller's own role, an external agent connecting via MCP can't see more than that role could already see through a normal SQL session.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of tools a single Snowflake-managed MCP server can expose, per this lesson?
questions.explain: The documentation caps a single MCP server at 50 tools, alongside other limits like a 250 KB response size and a recursion depth of 10.
